level1.text: A student stands $86.0\,\text{m}$ from the wall of a school and claps two wooden blocks together. The timing app of a phone measures that the echo returns $0.505\,\text{s}$ after the clap. What is the speed of sound according to the measurement?

A bat emits ultrasound for echolocation with a frequency of $45.0\,\text{kHz}$. What is the wavelength of the sound in air when the speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$? Give the answer in millimetres.

The fundamental frequency of the D string of a cello is $147\,\text{Hz}$. The string vibrates at the frequencies of the harmonic series at the same time. What is the frequency of the fourth member of the series, that is, the third overtone?

Extension task. An ice-cream van drives straight away from a listener at $15.0\,\text{m/s}$ and plays a melody, one note of which is $415\,\text{Hz}$. What frequency of this note does a listener at rest hear? The air is calm, and the speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$.

Classify the sounds as infrasound, audible sound or ultrasound: a) the lowest part of a thunder rumble, $12\,\text{Hz}$, b) a reference tuning note, $440\,\text{Hz}$, c) a dog whistle, $35\,\text{kHz}$, d) the sound of ultrasound imaging, $2.5\,\text{MHz}$. Justify using the limits.
level1.answer: a) infrasound; b) audible sound; c) ultrasound; d) ultrasound

level1.text: Two tuning forks sound one after the other in air. One sound seems clearly higher than the other, but both seem equally loud. Which of the following must be true of the higher sound?
level1.answer: Its frequency is greater, so the pressure varies more times per second.

choices.text: Its amplitude is greater, so the air pressure varies more strongly.
choices.feedback: Amplitude determines the loudness of a sound, not its pitch. In the problem the sounds seem equally loud, so the amplitudes can be the same even though the pitch is different.

choices.text: Its wavelength is longer, because a high-pitched sound travels faster in air.
choices.feedback: The speed of sound in air does not depend on frequency. When the speed is the same, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength $\lambda = \tfrac{v}{f}$, not a longer one.

choices.text: Its frequency is greater, so the pressure varies more times per second.
choices.feedback: Correct: pitch is determined by frequency. A higher sound means more vibrations per second, that is, a greater frequency $f$.

choices.text: Its period is longer, so one vibration takes longer.
choices.feedback: Period and frequency are reciprocals, $T = \tfrac{1}{f}$. The period of the higher sound is shorter, not longer.

level1.text: An ambulance drives at a steady speed straight towards a listener at rest, and the siren sounds all the time at its own constant frequency. The air is calm. How does the listener hear the pitch of the siren as the ambulance approaches?
level1.answer: Constant and higher than the siren's own, because the wavefronts are bunched up in front.

choices.text: Higher and higher the closer the car is, because the distance to the listener keeps getting shorter.
choices.feedback: This is a common misconception. The frequency heard depends on the speed of the car, not on its distance. When the speed is constant, the frequency heard is also constant. As the car approaches, the loudness of the sound grows, not the pitch.

choices.text: Exactly the siren's own frequency, because the motion of the car changes only the loudness of the sound.
choices.feedback: The siren vibrates all the time at the frequency $f_0$, but the listener meets the wavefronts more often, because the source moves after them. So the motion changes the frequency heard too, not only the loudness.

choices.text: Lower than the siren's own, because the motion of the car slows down the sound in air.
choices.feedback: The speed of sound in air does not depend on the motion of the source. In front of an approaching source the wavelength becomes shorter, so the frequency heard is greater, not smaller.

choices.text: Constant and higher than the siren's own, because the wavefronts are bunched up in front.
choices.feedback: Correct: the source moves after its own wavefronts, so the fronts are bunched up in front of it and the wavelength is shorter. The frequency heard $f = \tfrac{v}{\lambda}$ is therefore greater than $f_0$ and stays the same until the car passes the listener.

level1.text: Two tuning forks with frequencies $392\,\text{Hz}$ and $398\,\text{Hz}$ sound at the same time. How much time passes between two successive loud moments, that is, what is the period of the beats? Give the answer in seconds.

In the FFT spectrum of a note played on a violin there are peaks at the frequencies $330\,\text{Hz}$, $660\,\text{Hz}$, $990\,\text{Hz}$ and $1320\,\text{Hz}$. The strongest peak is at the frequency $660\,\text{Hz}$.

In another situation a listener stands right next to a straight road. A car drives at a steady speed straight towards the listener, passes the listener and moves straight away. The own frequency of the horn of the car is $400\,\text{Hz}$, and the air is calm.

The numbers are example values. Decide which statements are true and which are false.

statements.text: The note of the violin sounds as high as a pure tone of $660\,\text{Hz}$.
statements.feedback: False: the pitch is determined by the fundamental frequency, not by the strongest peak. The fundamental frequency is the lowest frequency of the harmonic series and the spacing of the peaks, $330\,\text{Hz}$.

statements.text: A flute playing the same note sounds different from the violin because its overtones have different strengths.
statements.feedback: True: the same note means the same fundamental frequency $330\,\text{Hz}$. The timbre depends on how strong the overtones are compared with the fundamental frequency, and it is different for different instruments.

statements.text: In front of an approaching car the sound of the horn travels faster in air than when the car stands still.
statements.feedback: False: the sound travels at the same speed relative to the air whether the source moves or not. The motion of the source changes the wavelength: in front of the car the wavefronts are closer together.

statements.text: During the approach the frequency that is heard keeps increasing as the car gets closer.
statements.feedback: False: the frequency that is heard depends on the speed of the car, not on the distance. At a steady speed the frequency is the same throughout the approach and higher than $400\,\text{Hz}$. As the car approaches, the loudness grows, not the pitch.

statements.text: After the car has passed, the listener hears the horn at a frequency lower than $400\,\text{Hz}$.
statements.feedback: True: behind a car that moves away the wavefronts are farther apart than when the car stands still, so the wavelength is longer and the frequency that is heard is lower than the own frequency of the horn.

level2.text: A piano tuner strikes a tuning fork with a frequency of $262\,\text{Hz}$ and at the same time plays a piano string that sounds slightly lower than the tuning fork. He counts $15$ loud moments, that is, beats, in $5.0\,\text{s}$. What is the frequency of the string?

A loudspeaker emits sound in air with a wavelength of $0.850\,\text{m}$. The sound passes from the surface of a lake into the water. What is the wavelength of the sound in water? The speed of sound in air is $340\,\text{m/s}$ and in water $1480\,\text{m/s}$.

Extension task. A driver drives at $90.0\,\text{km/h}$ straight towards a junction where a stationary warning siren sounds at $650\,\text{Hz}$. What frequency does the driver hear? The air is calm, and the speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$.

Extension task. The engine of a racing car sounds at $425\,\text{Hz}$ in the pit at rest. When the car drives at the same engine speed straight away from a spectator standing on the extension of the straight, the spectator hears the frequency $398\,\text{Hz}$. How fast is the car moving? The air is calm, and the speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$.

Extension task. A student standing beside the road records the sound of the horn of a car driving straight towards him. When the car is at rest, the frequency of the horn is $392\,\text{Hz}$. As the car approaches, the frequency is measured four times (example data).

The car drives at a steady speed. The air is calm, and the speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$. How fast is the car moving according to the mean of the measurements?

level2.text:
Extension task. A student solves a problem: a car drives at $30.0\,\text{m/s}$ straight towards a listener at rest and sounds a horn with a frequency of $500\,\text{Hz}$. The speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$.

The student uses the formula $f = f_0 \cdot \tfrac{v + v_\text{s}}{v}$ and gets the frequency heard $544\,\text{Hz}$.

What is the error in the student's solution? Calculate the correct frequency heard.
The figure shows the combined sound of two tuning forks sounding at the same time, measured with a microphone. What is the beat frequency? Read the necessary data from the figure.

level3.text:
Extension task. A listener stands right next to a straight road and measures with a phone app the frequency of the siren of a passing ambulance: $476\,\text{Hz}$ as the car approaches and $404\,\text{Hz}$ as it moves away. The speed of the ambulance is constant, but the siren's own frequency is not known.

How fast is the ambulance moving? The air is calm, and the speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$.

A guitarist plays the A string at the same time as a $440\,\text{Hz}$ reference note and hears a beat frequency of $4\,\text{Hz}$, that is, four loud moments every second. When she tightens the string slightly, the beat frequency grows to $6\,\text{Hz}$. What was the frequency of the string before tightening? Justify why the answer is unique.

A student measures the FFT spectrum of a low note of a clarinet. The spectrum has clear peaks at the frequencies $147\,\text{Hz}$, $441\,\text{Hz}$, $735\,\text{Hz}$ and $1029\,\text{Hz}$, and almost nothing in between. a) What is the fundamental frequency of the note? b) Which members of the harmonic series are missing from the spectrum? c) What does this tell about the standing wave of the air column of the clarinet?
level3.answer: Fundamental frequency $147\,\text{Hz}$; the even multiples ($294\,\text{Hz}$, $588\,\text{Hz}$, $882\,\text{Hz}$) are missing, so the air column vibrates like a tube closed at one end.

level3.text:
Extension task. A cardiologist measures the speed of blood flow with an ultrasound device (example data). The probe emits ultrasound with a frequency of $f_0 = 4.00\,\text{MHz}$ towards blood that flows straight towards the probe. The red blood cells reflect the sound back to the probe. The sound travels in tissue at $1540\,\text{m/s}$.

The probe measures the change in the frequency of the reflected sound, $\Delta f = f - f_0$, at different moments of the heartbeat.

What is the greatest measured speed of the blood? Treat the red blood cell first as a moving listener that receives the sound of the probe, and then as a moving source that emits the same frequency back. Justify briefly why the measured change is almost double compared with one Doppler shift.

data.caption: Example data: change in frequency during the heartbeat

level3.text:
A guitarist plucks a $0.650\,\text{m}$ long string in two ways: from the middle of the string and very close to the bridge. The sounds are recorded, and the peak frequencies and relative amplitudes are read from the FFT spectra (example data). In both spectra the amplitude of the fundamental frequency is marked as $1.00$.

a) What is the fundamental frequency of the string? Which harmonics are almost entirely missing when the string is plucked in the middle?

b) Calculate the speed of the wave in the string. Enter the result of this part in the answer box.

c) Explain why some of the harmonics are missing when plucking in the middle, and tell which way of plucking gives the brighter sound and why.
